conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you’re here. I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health clinician—my whole job is to support new mothers as they navigate the huge emotional shifts that can come after birth. Today I’d like to do a quick check-in using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a 10-question screening that helps us see how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past seven days. Nothing you share leaves this room, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you. We’ll move through each question one at a time, and if anything feels hard to talk about, we can pause or take it gently. Ready to start?

First, I’m wondering: over the past week, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you happy, or does everything feel a bit flat?

I mean... I still get little sparks of happiness, I guess. Like yesterday I managed to drink my favorite iced coffee while the baby napped, and for a minute it tasted the way it used to. But it fades fast—like the color’s been turned down. Most things feel kind of “meh,” even when I know I should be enjoying them.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, I can still laugh sometimes—like when my husband made that goofy face to quiet the baby. It’s just... the giggles don’t last long, and I have to work harder to find the funny side. A couple of evenings I caught myself smiling at a silly meme, but it feels more forced than it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to tell myself “tomorrow I’ll feel excited about getting outside for a walk,” but when morning comes, it just feels… flat—like I’m checking the box instead of actually wanting to do it. I still plan little things, hoping the spark will come back, but mostly I’m going through the motions.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Like if the baby’s extra fussy, I’ll think, “Maybe I’m not feeding him right,” or “I should’ve noticed he was overtired sooner.” Nothing huge, but little stuff keeps sticking in my head, telling me I should’ve known better.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes my mind just races ahead—like I’ll be rocking the baby and suddenly worry his breathing sounds weird, even though I just watched the pediatrician check him yesterday. It’s not constant, but every day or two a nervous thought pops up out of nowhere and I have to talk myself down.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky, no. I get that quick jolt of “what if something’s wrong?” but it settles pretty fast once I take a few breaths or check on the baby. No full-on scares or racing heart for no reason.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah—it feels like the laundry and the feeds and the texts I haven’t answered just pile up. I usually push through, but last night I looked at the sink full of bottles and wanted to sit on the floor instead of dealing with it. I still manage, but it takes more effort than it used to.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly. I do lie there feeling kind of heavy or blah, but once the light’s off I drift off in maybe 15-20 minutes. Only twice this week I tossed a bit longer because I kept replaying little worries, but I still got decent chunks of sleep when the baby let me.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah, I do feel that way some of the time. It’s not every moment—there are bright spots when the baby smiles or when my partner brings me tea—but a lot of the day there’s this low, gray sadness that just sits with me. I’ll be folding onesies and suddenly feel like I’m about to tear up for no clear reason. It’s not overwhelming, but it’s definitely there, more days than not.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried a couple of times this week—nothing huge, just quiet tears while I was washing bottles or when the baby wouldn’t settle. It’s not all-day sobbing, but yeah, the sadness leaks out maybe once a day, especially when I’m alone and everything feels a bit much.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I might feel low, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like “me” again, not disappear.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 15: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: Self-report on 10-item Edinburgh-based questionnaire (2 wks postpartum)

Symptoms / Observations  
- Persistent low mood (“low, gray sadness… more days than not”)  
- Marked anhedonia (pleasure markedly reduced; activities feel “flat,” “forced”)  
- Daily crying spells (quiet tears ≈ 1×/day when alone)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame over routine infant care  
- Recurrent, intrusive anxious thoughts about infant safety (no panic attacks)  
- Feeling overwhelmed by routine tasks; motivation notably reduced  
- Sleep onset modestly prolonged by rumination (no sustained insomnia)  
- No self-harm ideation (explicitly denied)

Pattern  
Symptoms present most days, interfere with enjoyment and coping, but patient continues to function and care for infant.

Screening Significance  
Findings consistent with mild–moderate postpartum depression with secondary anxiety features. Meets threshold for further assessment and possible referral; no safety concerns at present.

Risk Factors Documented  
- Persistent sadness & crying  
- Loss of pleasure  
- Self-blame / guilt  
- Being overwhelmed / reduced coping  
- Absence of suicidal ideation

Plan  
Recommend formal clinical interview (PHQ-9, GAD-7, EPDS) and consideration of evidence-based intervention; monitor safety at each contact.
